system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: Circle packing theorem
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: In scope: definition of circle packing and tangency graph, existence for finite simple planar graphs, uniqueness up to Mobius transformations and reflections for triangulations (and with prescribed outer radii), reduction to triangulations, and the outline of the radii and edge-length proof. Excluded: infinite-graph packings and the He-Schramm dichotomy.

ATOMS:
- MATH-PROB-C06-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Every finite simple planar graph $G$ has a circle packing, that is, there exists a circle packing $P$ such that the tangency graph $G(P)$ is isomorphic to $G$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0012-s15] Theorem 1.1 (Koebe 1936) Every finite simple planar graph G has a circle packing.
    [MATH-PROB-p0012-s16] That is, there exists a circle packing P such that G(P) is isomorphic to G.
- MATH-PROB-C06-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A circle packing is a collection of discs $P = \{C_v\}$ in the plane $\mathbb{C}$ such that any two distinct discs in $P$ have disjoint interiors, so that distinct discs may be tangent but may not overlap.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0012-s09] A circle packing is a collection of discs P = {Cv} in the plane C such that any two distinct discs in P have disjoint interiors.
    [MATH-PROB-p0012-s10] That is, distinct discs in P may be tangent, but may not overlap.
- MATH-PROB-C06-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: The tangency graph $G(P)$ of a circle packing $P$ is the graph whose vertex set is $P$ and in which two vertices are connected by an edge if and only if their corresponding circles are tangent.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0012-s11] Given a circle packing P, we define the tangency graph G(P) of P to be the graph with vertex set P and with two vertices connected by an edge if and only if their corresponding circles are tangent.
- MATH-PROB-C06-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: If $G$ is a finite triangulation, then the circle packing whose tangency graph is isomorphic to $G$ is unique, up to Möbius transformations and reflections in lines.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0014-s05] Claim 1.3 If G is a finite triangulation, then the circle packing whose tangency graph is isomorphic to G is unique, up to Möbius transformations and reflections in lines.
- MATH-PROB-C06-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: For a finite triangulation $G$ on vertex set $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ in which $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ form a face, and any three positive numbers $\rho_1,\rho_2,\rho_3$, the circle packing in which $C_1,C_2,C_3$ are mutually tangent, form the outer face, and have radii $\rho_1,\rho_2,\rho_3$ respectively is unique up to translations and rotations of the plane.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0046-s01] Theorem 3.6 Let G = (V, E) be a finite triangulation on vertex set V = {v1, . . . , vn} and assume that {v1, v2, v3} form a face.
    [MATH-PROB-p0046-s02] Then for any three positive numbers ρ1, ρ2, ρ3, there exists a circle packing C1, . . . , Cn as in Theorem 3.5 with the additional property that C1, C2, C3 are mutually tangent, form the outer face, and have radii ρ1, ρ2, ρ3, respectively.
    [MATH-PROB-p0046-s03] Furthermore, this circle packing is unique, up to translations and rotations of the plane.
- MATH-PROB-C06-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: To obtain a circle packing of a finite planar map from the triangulation case, one adds a single vertex inside each face connected to all vertices bounding that face, which yields a triangulation, applies the circle packing theorem for triangulations, and then removes the circles of the added vertices, leaving a circle packing of the original map that respects its cyclic permutations.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0045-s05] Indeed, in any planar map we may add a single vertex inside each face and connect it to all vertices bounding that face.
    [MATH-PROB-p0045-s06] The obtained map is a triangulation, and after applying the circle packing theorem for triangulations, we may remove the circles corresponding to the added vertices, obtaining a circle packing of the original map which respects its cyclic permutations.
- MATH-PROB-C06-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Uniqueness of a circle packing cannot be expected for finite simple planar graphs in general, since in an example graph some circles can be slid along another circle while the packing remains a circle packing of the same graph.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0014-s01] We cannot expect a uniqueness statement in Theorem 1.1 (see Fig. 1.1; we may “slide” circles 5 and 6 along circle 2).
- MATH-PROB-C06-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The tangency graph $G(P)$ of any circle packing $P$ is simple, meaning any two vertices are connected by at most one edge and no edge begins and ends at the same vertex.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0012-s13] It is also clear from the definition that G(P) is simple, that is, any two vertices are connected by at most one edge and there are no edges beginning and ending at the same vertex.
- MATH-PROB-C06-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: A planar triangulation is a planar graph that can be drawn so that every face is incident to exactly three edges, and when the graph is finite this property must hold for the outer face as well.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MATH-PROB-p0014-s03] Definition 1.2 A planar triangulation is a planar graph that can be drawn so that every face is incident to exactly three edges.
    [MATH-PROB-p0014-s04] In particular, when the graph is finite this property must hold for the outer face as well.
